title: Standardized patient: a cough
intro: Your first standardized-patient encounter. The coordinator hands you the door card: Mr. Daniel Reyes, 58, "cough". You have ten minutes; a camera records it for your feedback session.

steps.say: You knock, wait for "Come in," and open the door. A man in his late fifties sits on the edge of the exam table, coughing into his elbow.

options.text: "Good morning. I'm a first-year medical student working with the team today. What would you like me to call you?"
options.reply: "Danny's fine. Nice to meet you." He relaxes a little.
He blinks. "Uh, who are you?" You've skipped the introduction.

options.text: You sit at the computer and start typing. "Name and date of birth?"
options.reply: He answers the back of your head. You've lost eye contact before you've started.

choice.lesson: Introduce yourself and your role, and ask how the patient would like to be addressed

choice.prompt: Your first question about why he's here:

options.reply: "This cough. It just won't quit." He tells you in his own words.
"No." He waits for the next question. A closed question gives you a closed answer.
He stiffens. "How did you know that?" It sounds like a judgment.

history.opening: "I've had this cough for about six weeks now, and it isn't going away."

items.ask: When did the cough start, and how has it changed?
items.answer: "Six weeks ago, after a cold. The cold went away; the cough didn't. If anything it's worse."

items.ask: Are you bringing anything up? What does it look like?
items.answer: "Yellowish phlegm in the mornings. And twice last week there were streaks of blood in it. That scared me."

items.ask: Have you had fevers, chills or night sweats?
items.answer: "No fevers. No sweats that I've noticed."

items.ask: Have you lost any weight without trying?
items.answer: "My belt's looser. Maybe ten pounds since the summer, and I'm not dieting."

items.ask: Any shortness of breath or chest pain?
items.answer: "A bit winded on the stairs lately. No real chest pain."

items.ask: Do you have any medical conditions?

items.answer: "Lisinopril, for the pressure. About a year now."

items.ask: Do you smoke, or have you ever smoked?
items.answer: "Since I was eighteen. A pack a day. I've tried to quit a few times."
"Twenty years at the shipyard, then delivery driving."

items.ask: Any contact with tuberculosis, or time in a shelter or prison?
Any illnesses that run in your family?
items.answer: "My dad had emphysema. My sister had breast cancer."

items.ask: What worries you most about the cough?
items.answer: He looks at his hands. "That it's cancer. My dad smoked too."

choice.prompt: He said he's afraid it's cancer. How do you respond?

options.text: "That's a very understandable worry. Can you tell me more about it? I'll make sure the doctor hears it, and we'll look into it properly."
options.reply: He nods. "Thanks. I've been scared to say it out loud."

options.text: "Oh, I'm sure it's nothing. Probably just a bad cold."
options.reply: He looks unconvinced. False reassurance can't be kept, and he knows you can't know that.

options.text: "Well, with your smoking, it could well be cancer."
options.reply: He goes pale. A frightening guess from a student isn't what he needs.

choice.lesson: Acknowledge and explore the patient's concerns rather than reassuring falsely

choice.prompt: Time is nearly up. How do you close?

options.text: Summarize what he's told you, ask if you've missed anything, and explain that the doctor will come in to talk about next steps.
options.reply: "That's it exactly. Thank you for listening." He shakes your hand.

options.text: "OK, that's all my questions. The doctor will be in."
options.reply: He's left not knowing what happens next.

options.text: You thank him and leave while he's still talking.
options.reply: The door closes on his sentence.

choice.lesson: Close by summarizing, checking for anything missed, and explaining next steps

steps.say: The coordinator calls time. In the hallway, your preceptor, Dr. Farah Siddiqui, has watched on camera.
"The history is the most powerful test we have," she says. "You just did your first one. Let's watch the recording together."
steps.speaker: Dr. Farah Siddiqui

feedback: "Excellent. You let him talk, you found the red flags, and you heard his fear. That's the job."
"A good start. Watch the recording for where you could have asked more openly."
"First encounters are hard. We'll practice the structure together before the next one."
